sources.title: He-Man and the Masters of the Universe: Dragon Pearl of Destruction launches February 4, 2027
sources.text: Side-scrolling beat’ em up game He-Man and the Masters of the Universe: Dragon Pearl of Destruction will launch for PlayStation 5 , Xbox Series , PlayStation 4 , Xbox One , Switch , and PC via Steam on February 4, 2027 for $29.99 / €29.99, publisher Limited Run Games and developer Bitmap Bureau announced. Physical edition pre-orders are available now via Limited Run Games . Here is an overview of the game, via Limited Run Games: Inspired by the iconic ’80s cartoon, He-Man and the Masters of the Universe: Dragon Pearl of Destruction allows players to take control of Eternia’s beloved heroes, including He-Man, Teela, Man-At-Arms, and more, to battle Skeletor and Evil-Lyn and save Eternia from plunging into darkness. Fight through over 13 action-packed levels using character-specific moves, abilities, and power-ups to stop Skeletor’s ancient ritual that threatens to take over Eternia. Battle Cat, He-Man’s fearless feline companion, also joins the fray, battling on the side of justice with his claws unsheathed.

sources.name: GamesRadar
sources.title: He-Man and the Masters of the Universe Dragon Pearl of Destruction's lunchbox is a perfect '80s throwback
sources.text: He-Man and the Masters of the Universe Dragon Pearl of Destruction is a Bitmap Bureau-developed (in collaboration with Mattel) game that brings the iconic 80s cartoon to life as a Streets of Rage-style brawler. With its collector's edition being handled by Limited Run Games, there was no denying that the game would be bundled with a feast of physical merch, but I wasn't expecting a throwback quite like a lunchbox. The $99.99 (via Limited Run Games) Collector's Edition, no matter if it's the Switch, PS5, or Xbox version, includes the plastic lunchbox, which feels just as equivalently '80s as the original series. Growing up, I often received my cousin's lunchboxes as hand-me-downs, and a metal He-Man lunchbox was a staple of their childhood, and later mine. All it's missing is a matching Thermos flask and the faint smell of old fruit and salt and shake crisps to be one of the most truly nostalgic collector edition releases. Pre-orders for the He-Man and the Masters of the Universe Dragon Pearl of Destruction Collector's Edition are available now through November 22, 11:59 PM ET. If you want more unique collector's editions based on iconic Mattel toys, Barbie Rewind pre-orders are available for £59.99 at Amazon, and the Deluxe Edition includes a full-sized Barbie doll. Saturday Mornings in my '90s childhood were often spent having to use my cousin's hand-me-downs, and He-Man (and She-Ra) were a big part of that. Often it was the toys and old videotapes that made their way into my possession, but lunchboxes were also commonplace, which is why I'm pretty privy to this Limited Run Games release. Often the brand's fancy collector's editions include statues of varying quality, and this one is not exempt. There is a 4.9-inch Mini Power Sword and an acrylic standee showing He-Man riding Battle Cat included, but the lunchbox feels the most authentic. In fact, despite it not being included as a numbered release, this lunchbox puts this version up there as one of the better editions I've seen from the retailer. I'd much sooner have it in my collection than the falling-apart statuette included with my Limited Run Games ClockTower Rewind release. It's nice to see that despite all the physical tat that's bundled within its $99.99 MSRP, which also includes a pin set and a mini comic book, there's a physical copy of the game too. If you pre-order this collector's edition, you also get a physical copy of the game on the platform of your choice, and an alternative steel case to keep it in. Rockstar should maybe be taking notes if they choose to give the GTA 6 Collector's Edition another shot. If you are thinking of grabbing this collector's edition, I recommend pre-ordering sooner rather than later. While the pre-order window remains open until November 22, these Limited Run Games releases can be perfect fodder for eBay resellers. Love securing games as soon as possible? Check out our GTA 6 pre-order and Legend of Zelda Ocarina of Time pre-order pages. Hardware nerds unite, sign up to our free tech newsletter for a weekly digest of the hottest new tech, the latest gadgets on the test bench, and much more from the team at GamesRadar+. Ever since I first held a NES controller in my hand I've been obsessed with gaming, and the hardware it runs on. I could hook up a NES and SNES to a telly, without instructions, before I could walk. Even now, nothing is more exciting then taking a console, or handheld, out the box for the first time and setting it up. This obsession transformed into a love of games and game music, which lead to my music degree and dream of becoming the Scottish Nobuo Uematsu. After sharing my love of games through music, I began to share my love through words on sites like TechRadar and iMore. This lead to becoming a Hardware staff writer for PCGamesN, and later the Senior Tech Writer for Dexerto, covering all things Steam Deck, PlayStation and Nintendo. With that experience, I was able to level up as Hardware Editor for GamesRadar+, where I'm still just as Nintendo, PlayStation and gaming tech obsessed as ever. sources.title: Sifu será lançado para Android e iOS em outubro; veja trailer do port
sources.text: Sifu , jogo de artes marciais da Sloclap, será lançado para Android e iOS. A desenvolvedora anunciou a versão mobile do game, com estreia prevista para 12 de outubro deste ano. “A mesma ação, a mesma aura, a mesma atmosfera. Agora, na palma da sua mão”, anunciou a Sloclap no X. Na mesma publicação, a empresa anexou um trailer de gameplay da nova versão. A jogatina de Sifu no mobile parece ser idêntica à versão para PC e consoles, com os mesmos cenários, personagens e chefões – portanto, tudo indica que seja um port. No vídeo, são exibidos os botões virtuais adaptados para a tela touchscreen, que permitirão experimentar a porradaria mesmo sem um controle dedicado . Sifu é um jogo de artes marciais com combate rápido, em que o jogador acompanha o protagonista em uma jornada de vingança. O combate é cheio de combos interessantes e marcado pelo forte foco em parries e desvios. Porém, o que deixou Sifu mais relevante é o sistema de vidas. Durante as fases, cada morte do personagem principal não é necessariamente fatal, mas faz com que ele envelheça alguns anos – o que o deixa mais forte com o tempo, mas também mais frágil. O game over acontece quando o protagonista fica velho demais para retornar após uma derrota. Reconhecido jogo de artes marciais da Sloclap, Sifu foi lançado para PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5 e PC em fevereiro de 2022; chegou ao Nintendo Switch meses depois e, em 2023, foi lançado para Xbox One e Xbox Series X | S. O jogo já está listado na App Store e na Play Store. No iOS, vai custar US$ 7,99 (R$ 39,80, em conversão direta) ; no Android, o preço ainda não aparece na loja, mas já é possível fazer o pré-registro, que notifica o usuário quando o jogo estiver pronto para download. O jogo conquistou uma boa nota na análise do Voxl anos atrás . Ao longo do tempo, muito conteúdo foi adicionado ao game, incluindo novas arenas, cosméticos desbloqueáveis e mais desafios que estendem as horas de conteúdo. Quer ficar por dentro das novidades do mundo dos games? Acesse o Voxl e acompanhe as últimas notícias sobre Sifu , jogos mobile e lançamentos. 4 apps pagos estão de graça para baixar na Play Store; confira Apple lança HomeView, display inteligente com Siri AI para casa e lazer Nova política da Anthropic proíbe você de ser ‘cruel’ com o Claude Apple lança campainhas, câmeras e termostatos inteligentes em coleção para a casa Empresários recebem boleto DDA ‘falso’ sem serviço contratado ou prestado

stories.title: 'Our humble goal is to survive the AI revolution' says Epic Games CEO, as its Star Wars and Marvel crossover pivots to 'AI first' development
stories.summary: Art will be "generated with full AI workflows".

sources.name: PC Gamer
sources.title: 'Our humble goal is to survive the AI revolution' says Epic Games CEO, as its Star Wars and Marvel crossover pivots to 'AI first' development
sources.text: Art will be "generated with full AI workflows". An unannounced Star Wars and Marvel shooter in the works at Epic Games has been delayed, and its creators instructed to take an "AI first" approach to development. Staff were advised of the pivot last week, according to a Bloomberg report, with the project delayed indefinitely from its (unannounced) March 2027 release. That "AI first" approach seems pretty comprehensive: the instructions per Bloomberg are to "implement an 'AI first' production model using tools such as Anthropic's Claude". Art will be "generated with full AI workflows", according to the same set of instructions. Shortly after Bloomberg's report was published, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney took to X to share his own thoughts: Epic Games laid off over 1,000 employees in March, citing the decline in console sales, Epic's ongoing legal disputes with Apple and Google, and difficulty in delivering "consistent Fortnite magic with every season". Let's be honest: a Marvel and Star Wars crossover shooter made by Epic Games, predominantly utilising generative AI and AI workflows, will be a pretty fascinating experiment to behold. It's such a rich intersection of exhaustingly ubiquitous pop culture touchstones that there's every possibility its AI origins will be less detectable than they might otherwise be. Because AI slop already mostly looks like Fortnite, Star Wars and Marvel. Add Pixar (which Fortnite looks like), and you basically have slop Mount Rushmore. This is the abyss staring back into the abyss. Sweeney's quote about audiences wishing they were still in 2016 is telling. The AI industry loves to frame uptake of the technology as an inevitability that detractors / luddites will just need to cope with, or at least, they do when they're not loudly worrying that the technology might kill us . From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews Still, terrible things that no one likes do have a way of bleeding inescapably into our everyday lives. Tech companies own platforms best equipped to make us tolerate things we innately abhor. People hated Facebook's rollout of "likes"—now most of us "like" things with our mouths firmly closed. People hated it when social media feeds stopped being feeds, so that, for example, weird videos about putting various objects through meat grinders are now mainstream. The transformation from "way to catch up with friends" into "ruinously addictive habit" wasn't appreciated, but it's the norm now anyway. In other words, the tech industry knows that it doesn't matter whether you like it or not: you'll get what you're given. Shaun Prescott is the Australian editor of PC Gamer. With over ten years experience covering the games industry, his work has appeared on GamesRadar+, TechRadar, The Guardian, PLAY Magazine, the Sydney Morning Herald, and more. Specific interests include indie games, obscure Metroidvanias, speedrunning, experimental games and FPSs. He thinks Lulu by Metallica and Lou Reed is an all-time classic that will receive its due critical reappraisal one day. sources.title: Xbox insists it’s not giving up on original IP: ‘We won’t survive if we only relive the past’
sources.text: Despite doubling down on its biggest franchises, Asha Sharma insists original IP is important Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has insisted that Microsoft hasnât given up on creating original IP, despite doubling down on its biggest franchises in a division reset. Since her appointment earlier this year, Sharma has enacted a sweeping overhaul of Xbox âs content strategy, laying off thousands of staff and closing or divesting numerous first-party studios. The company âresetâ has been viewed as a doubling down on Xboxâs biggest franchises. Notably, Halo has been moved to the stewardship of Call of Duty publisher Activision , Obsidian has been put to work on a new Fallout under Bethesda , while studios like Double Fine ( Kiln ), Ninja Theory (Hellblade), and Compulsion ( South of Midnight ) have been divested. However, speaking during an internal Town Hall meeting this week, obtained by Windows Central , Sharma claimed that creating original games was still important for the gaming divisionâs future, despite axing some of its most prolific creators of IP. “On content, I think this is probably the thing that you are all seeing the most about as we’re making a lot of changes,” Sharma reportedly said. “We’re backing our strongest franchises. I want our great games to become great global billion-dollar franchises. I would also like to see us continue to create enduring new IP. We will not survive if we only revive on the past. We have to find new ways, and courage, to have invention on new IP, that reaches new sets of audiences.” Sharma recently denied the gaming division could be sold by Microsoft , following her streamlining of the business this year. Earlier this summer, a report by The Information claimed that Microsoft was considering spinning out or restructuring its gaming division as a wholly owned subsidiary. This would, in theory, make Xbox easier to sell off in the future. However, in the new interview with the New York Times , Sharma has denied that any such plans exist. âXbox is not for sale,â Sharma told the publication. âWe will do whatever it takes to set the company up for success, and we will look at the right partnerships, the right operating model and everything needed to achieve that.â

sources.name: GamesRadar
sources.title: Xbox boss Asha Sharma says "we will not survive" if devs don't create "enduring new IP"
sources.text: This comes after multiple new Xbox games were canceled amid restructuring As Xbox continues to struggle, CEO Asha Sharma has reportedly stated her desire to keep making "enduring new IP" rather than solely relying on the past, as the company "will not survive" if it does. Xbox is still in the midst of ongoing restructuring, with it announced in early July that 3,200 people were set to be laid off by the end of the financial year, and multiple Xbox-owned studios have been impacted in other ways . Compulsion Games, Undead Labs, and Double Fine have gone independent, while two agreements for Ninja Theory have fallen through, and consultation is still underway at Arkane . Sharma admitted in July that the current Xbox is not "healthy," and even looking from the outside, it's not hard to see that. Per transcripts shared with Windows Central , in a recent company town hall meeting, Sharma reportedly acknowledged the large amount of changes being made to Xbox's content. "We're backing our strongest franchises. I want our great games to become great global billion-dollar franchises," she is quoted as saying. However, she apparently notes that the company can't just rely on old favorites. "I would also like to see us continue to create enduring new IP," she continues, adding that "we will not survive" if we only lean on the past. "We have to find new ways, and courage, to have invention on new IP, that reaches new sets of audiences," she adds. While there's definitely truth to what she's saying, it's hard not to find the sentiment somewhat odd when it follows multiple game cancellations at Xbox. Last year, for example, a gorgeous new game from Rare, Everwild , was shelved along with Project Blackbird , a new MMO project that was in development at Elder Scrolls Online developer ZeniMax Online Studios. More recently, Ninja Theory's Project Mara – an experimental horror project – was also scrapped . One thing that's sure to be in the company's favor, however, is that it's now not only publishing Hideo Kojima 's upcoming horror game , OD , but his Metal Gear Solid spiritual successor Physint , too. Sony was set to cancel the latter, prompting Kojima to seek another publisher in the form of the PlayStation maker's biggest rival. Hideo Kojima says Xbox had "never seen" anything like Physint, which is impressive considering it was the only publisher that didn't think his OD pitch was "crazy." Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more I'm GamesRadar+'s Deputy News Editor, working alongside the rest of the news team to deliver cool gaming stories that we love. After spending more hours than I can count filling The University of Sheffield's student newspaper with Pokemon and indie game content, and picking up a degree in Journalism Studies, I started my career at GAMINGbible where I worked as a journalist for over a year and a half. I then became TechRadar Gaming's news writer, where I sourced stories and wrote about all sorts of intriguing topics. In my spare time, you're sure to find me on my Nintendo Switch or PS5 playing through story-driven RPGs like Xenoblade Chronicles and Persona 5 Royal, nuzlocking old Pokemon games, or going for a Victory Royale in Fortnite. sources.name: PC Gamer
sources.title: Hundreds of layoffs and many cancelled projects later, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma reportedly says 'we will not survive' without new IPs
sources.text: Having one's cake and eating it too is meant to be a metaphor. Thousands of layoffs , a couple of booted studios, and a re-organisation of Obsidian away from its newer projects and onto Fallout later, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has reportedly taken to an internal town hall and talked about the importance of new IP. The transcript, as shared by Windows Central , goes as follows: "We're backing our strongest franchises. I want our great games to become great global billion-dollar franchises. I would also like to see us continue to create enduring new IP. We will not survive if we only revive [sic] on the past. We have to find new ways, and courage, to have invention on new IP, that reaches new sets of audiences." This is, to put it gently, very confusing. As part of Xbox's "Reset", the studio has done the following: That doesn't smack to me of the kind of courage and new IP invention that Sharma is talking about—most of these studios had either just made interesting new IPs (South of Midnight) or are in the business of doing cool, inventive new stuff (Double Fine). From a numbers-driven, capitalistic point of view, were they making bank? Likely not, but the phrase "trying to have your cake and eat it too" exists for a reason. The mouth isn't talking about what the hand is doing—waxing lyrical about courage and new IP while making some of the most cutthroat industry cuts we've seen in an already-dire decade. The one counterpoint to this is that Xbox has picked up Hideo Kojima's Physint . Which is technically a new IP. Not an IP that Xbox personally funded the most of, and it's being created by a beloved auteur, but hey. There is that. All of this isn't to say what seems to be Xbox's actual strategy—"backing our strongest franchises", as Sharma puts it—isn't understandable from that same ruthless abacus point of view. But given how sore its existing developers understandably feel from the sword dangling over their heads? I'd leave that town hall very confused. He made his start as a freelancer, writing for websites like Techradar, The Escapist, Dicebreaker, The Gamer, Into the Spine—and of course, PC Gamer. He'll sink his teeth into anything that looks interesting, though he has a soft spot for RPGs, soulslikes, roguelikes, deckbuilders, MMOs, and weird indie titles. He also plays a shelf load of TTRPGs in his offline time. Don't ask him what his favourite system is, he has too many. sources.name: Polygon
sources.title: Xbox 'Won’t Survive' Without New IP, CEO Says
sources.text: As Xbox continues its major “reset,” which has led to at least 1,600 job cuts and divestment from several studios , Xbox CEO Asha Sharma recently said in internal company communications that the division will “not survive” without new IP. While this statement would be affirming on its own, it rings a bit hollow given how thoroughly Xbox has gutted many of the teams behind its most interesting fresh series. Sharma made the statement in an Xbox town hall last week, and Windows Central obtained unauthorized transcripts of the talk. “On content, I think this is probably the thing that you are all seeing the most about as we’re making a lot of changes,” Sharma reportedly said. “We’re backing our strongest franchises. I want our great games to become great global billion-dollar franchises.” As part of Xbox’s massive changes, the division is clearly doubling down on existing big hits. The company is moving development of the Halo series to Call of Duty publisher Activision , which has a track record of consistently delivering new releases (of vastly varying quality). Additionally, Obsidian Entertainment is being moved under Bethesda as it works on a new Fallout game. However, Sharma's next point is a bit confusing given the company’s recent actions. “I would also like to see us continue to create enduring new IP. We will not survive if we only revive the past. We have to find new ways, and courage, to have invention on new IP, that reaches new sets of audiences.” While she is certainly correct, and no publisher can live forever on past glories, it’s ironic to say that after cutting ties with teams like Double Fine, Ninja Theory, Compulsion Games, and Undead Labs, all of which created new IP for Microsoft. Microsoft stopped funding all four studios, three of which have pulled off management buyouts to avoid shutdowns ( Ninja Theory is currently the odd one out) . Double Fine is known for out-there concepts , having released both Kiln , a multiplayer action game centered on pottery, and Keeper , where you play as a sentient lighthouse, over the last two years. Ninja Theory created the Hellblade series, and Undead Labs worked on State of Decay. Compulsion Games put out one of Microsoft’s most interesting recent titles, South of Midnight , a fantastical action-adventure set in the American South with an aesthetic inspired by stop-motion animation. Arkane Studios, which is currently in negotiations with Microsoft over its future , gave Xbox the brain-bending Deathloop and is currently working on Marvel’s Blade . For the studios that weren’t cut, things don’t look much better. By moving studios like Obsidian under Bethesda, the implication is that Obsidian won’t be able to make unique games like Pentiment because it will be busy working on Fallout and Elder Scrolls sequels. Microsoft reportedly slashed id Software to half of its former size , making Doom follow-ups a tall order. Essentially, Sharma’s words do not match the company’s actions. While it’s possible that when she says “new IP,” she means a new live-service or multiplayer game that hits millions of players, her comments read as hypocritical given Microsoft’s recent actions.

sources.name: PlayStation Blog
sources.title: Escape Academy 2: Back 2 School comes to PS5 on November 5
sources.text: Discover a fully explorable and puzzling open-world campus that rewards curiosity Hello Puzzlers and PlayStation fans! The team at Coin Crew Games is excited to share that Escape Academy 2: Back 2 School will be coming to PS5 on November 5. To celebrate, we are sharing some deep-dive information about what players can expect in this sequel that expands the first game from a more linear narrative to a whole new open-world campus. Of course, you can also expect couch or online co-op play available from the get go between the full campus, story and all of its puzzles. Whether you played the first game or not, Escape Academy 2: Back 2 School is open to everyone and represents a more fully-realized campus experience. We want the Academy to feel like a place players can get lost in, filled with characters, quests, secrets, and plenty of reasons to explore between escapes. Our campus is broken up into several distinct sections, each filled to the brim with quests and puzzles for you to encounter throughout the journey. For this lesson, we’re sharing new details on the Headmaster’s Tower and Humanities Campus, which makes a more expanded return from the first game after [spoiler!] Quanty burned down the library in the first game. The Headmaster’s Tower was one of the first spaces we worked on when designing the updated visuals in Escape Academy 2: Back 2 School and it inspired the most discussion about how to make a space feel truly “Academic” and further push the worldbuilding before expanding on each location’s unique identities. Players will get a sense of the Academy’s history more than ever with this area while still discovering plenty of playful and strange puzzles. This also led us back to the Headmaster’s Office, which was the setting of our very first escape in the original Escape Academy. The location became our visual target as we began leveling up the art style for Escape Academy 2: Back 2 School. We hope players will see how we pushed the visual identity of the Academy further while still making it recognizable to returning players. From concepts to being fully realized, the Humanities Campus has seen the most deviation from the first entry’s 2D map layout. It was a fun challenge designing this game to be more open world as we went through a lot of iteration with this area. At first, things felt too open, and we eventually found lots of new ways for players to engage with the area like interactable landmarks, side quests and escapes. As the art director, one of my favorite parts of building the game has been making the world itself part of the experience. Puzzles aren’t strictly limited to rooms anymore. This campus itself will reward you for staying curious. Because part of the Humanities Campus had to be rebuilt after the first game’s story, I expanded on the classical architecture inspiration from the original game’s library design. Compared to the rough and gritty industrial vibes of the Science Campus, or the colorful Arts Campus, I wanted to give this area a cozier feel, that might encourage a quiet coffee break or a philosophical puzzle discussion amongst students, while still inspiring some sense of mystery and discovery between its faculty offices, classrooms and library. You won’t have access to the Humanities Campus right away, but you’ll catch glimpses of it often with a striking keyhole-shaped fountain that can be seen across some of the best sightseeing spots on campus for you and the other students. This is intentional as we designed the campus itself to be its own living, breathing puzzle for you to unravel; we want exploration to feel as rewarding as puzzle-solving. Our hope is to create moments where players see something interesting before they understand how to reach it. We also hid a lot of keyhole embellishments all around the Academy, see if you can find them all. That’s all for today’s lesson. The team and I are thrilled to be bringing Escape Academy 2: Back 2 School back to PlayStation fans around the world when the game launches for PlayStation 5 on November 5. We can’t wait for players to explore the Academy, uncover its secrets, meet new and returning faces, and discover that there’s much more to this school than meets the eye. Stay tuned for more updates about the game.

sources.name: Gematsu
sources.title: Escape Academy 2: Back 2 School adds PS5 version, launches November 5
sources.text: Puzzle adventure game sequel Escape Academy 2: Back 2 School will launch for PlayStation 5 , Xbox Series , and PC via Steam , Epic Games Store , and Microsoft Store on November 5, publisher iam8bit and developer Coin Crew Games announced. It will also be available via Game Pass. The PlayStation 5 version is newly announced. Here is an overview of the game, via ima8bit: Escape Academy 2: Back 2 School is the sequel to the award-winning Escape Academy , enjoyed by over four million players! Welcome to Escape Academy, the world’s foremost clandestine educator in the art of Escape. Whether you’re a returning student or a new pupil, you’ve come to the right place. Escape Academy 2: Back 2 School evolves the escape room format of the first game into a whole new GENRE: This is the first open world escape room game, and it’s available right in the comfort of your own home. Digital Escape Rooms Designed by Masters of the Craft Escape Academy 2: Back 2 School features an all-new campaign boasting handcrafted, best-in-class escape rooms built by our team of veteran puzzle designers. But unlike real-life escape rooms, the puzzles in Escape Academy aren’t bound by those stuffy safety regulations: Spiked ceilings? Check. 100 foot drops? Check. And, most-dreaded of all… Final exams? Double check. The curriculum here at the Academy is equal parts life-threatening and wacky, because what better way to learn than while confronting one’s mortality. In Escape Academy 2: Back 2 School , the campus is one big puzzle room. Between classes, explore a sprawling, secret-filled hub with mysterious passage ways, hidden tunnels, and dangerous traps. Or chill out with your pals and take in all the *vibes* that student life has to offer. Whatever the case, the Academy’s your new home away from home. Grab a Classmate and Get Escapin’ With Online or Couch Cooperative Play Escaping with a friend has never been this fun. In a recent interview with GQ , Barone said that...

sources.name: GameSpot
sources.title: Haunted Chocolatier Is For “The People In Stardew Valley That Go Into The Mines”

sources.name: Eurogamer
sources.title: Stardew Valley creator's new game, Haunted Chocolatier, is "more of an action RPG" than farming sim
sources.text: "It's for the people that go into the mines." Stardew Valley creator Eric Barone, has given a new interview - and finally revealed a little more information about his upcoming title, Haunted Chocolatier. In a wide-ranging interview with GQ , which tackles topics ranging from creative burnout to the importance of 'cosy gaming', Barone also slips in some new information about what we can expect from his highly-anticipated Stardew Valley follow-up. And it's all rather surprising. Per the interview, this game is a much more action-oriented affair than the cosy homesteading of Stardew Valley: "It is still what I call a town game," he told GQ, "but it's more of an action RPG - the main focus is more about adventuring, finding equipment and getting more powerful. There are monsters, there are boss fights." For anyone that's played Stardew Valley, this won't be a massive shock; there is a combat element to the game, though mostly it's sequestered to one portion of the map - the mines that hold some of the game's rarest materials. If you had fun venturing in there at night to fight slimes and horde minerals, you're going to like Haunted Chocolatier, it seems. "[The new game] is for the people in Stardew Valley that go into the mines. That's what I do, honestly," said Barone. Elsewhere, Barone noted that Haunted Chocolatier is a more "metaphysical" experience than Stardew Valley - which makes sense, I suppose, given its connection to the world of ghosts and spirits - and that "no one's playing the game until I'm ready to show it". Hence, there's still no word on a solid release date. The last update we had on the game was all the way back in January, where Barone noted "I'm alive, the game is still in development" , following up previous statements he made alluding to the fact that the world of Haunted Chocolatier is bigger than Stardew Valley. As for when it's coming out? "The bottom line is, I don’t want to give a release date," Barone said at the start of the year. "The game will come out when it's done." If you want to learn more about the man behind one of video gaming's biggest phenomena of the past few generations, I'd urge you to read the full GQ piece: it's a sensitive, comprehensive look at a man that boasts many talents, yet is also humble and grounded. If you're interested in the musical side of his development process, I profiled Barone once in my column at The Guardian.

stories.title: Elon Musk dressing up as Wario for SNL "did not go over well" at Nintendo, ex-marketing leads say
stories.summary: Not anyone's finest hour, I don't think

sources.name: GamesRadar
sources.title: Elon Musk dressing up as Wario for SNL "did not go over well" at Nintendo, ex-marketing leads say
sources.text: The bastion of comedy that is Saturday Night Live recently decided to poke fun at the close-by release dates of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake and GTA 6 . The sketch marks the rare occasion the show acknowledges video games, bringing to mind a moment in 2021 where Elon Musk, of all people, showed up in a Wario suit. If you need a reminder, Musk hosted Saturday Night Live on May 8, 2021, and one of the bits involved a lawyer defending Wario in court against the accusation he murdered Mario. Yeah, I don't know either. The Tesla CEO himself was positioned as the villain of Super Mario Land 2: 6 Golden Coins, in a get up that included the moustache and all. Discussing SNL's latest venture into games satire, Kit Ellis and Krysta Yang, both former senior marketing staff at the house of Mario and Zelda, looked back at the reaction to the Musk-led skit. "They did not like the Elon Musk 2021 [bit]," Yang says, in an episode of Kit and Krysta , the podcast they share. "We were still there for that," Ellis points out. "That did not go over well," Yang states, as Ellis concurs that it "was not beloved" with a laugh. "That one was out of left field," Ellis observes. "There was no actual Nintendo product that connected to it." He mentions that "some of" the material was "getting into subject material that was uncomfortable for Nintendo." The whole thing is misguided, in my view. Wario's only ever been in direct opposition to Mario once - Bowser's the jumping plumber's actual arch-nemesis. Wario is just a bumbling, money-hungry inflection of Mario's cheeriness. A courtroom drama is deeply antithetical to the spirit of either character, too. The former Nintendo marketing leads point out in the conversation that the latest scene is more likely to have made execs smile, if only because it's potentially potent marketing they didn't have to pay for. Ultimately, that's all that matters really - unless Musk is involved, anyway. Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week The new Ocarina of Time figures are nowhere to be found, but some of the best Zelda amiibo are back at Nintendo UK Anthony is an Irish entertainment and games journalist, now based in Glasgow. He previously served as Senior Anime Writer at Dexerto and News Editor at The Digital Fix, on top of providing work for Variety, IGN, Den of Geek, PC Gamer, and many more. Besides Studio Ghibli, horror movies, and The Muppets, he enjoys action-RPGs, heavy metal, and pro-wrestling. He interviewed Animal once, not that he won’t stop going on about it or anything. sources.name: Eurogamer
sources.title: "That was not received well at Nintendo" - as GTA 6 and Zelda are lampooned by Saturday Night Live, former employees recall Elon Musk Wario skit controversy
sources.text: As American comedy series Saturday Night Live airs a sketch lampooning the November showdown between Grand Theft Auto 6 and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, a pair of former Nintendo employees have recalled a more infamous SNL sketch from years earlier that did not go down well at all. The older SNL sketch had controversial billionaire businessman Elon Musk dress as Nintendo character Wario, on trial for being evil, ironically enough. During the trial there were mentions of Mario taking drugs, blurred out Luigi dick pics, all while Wario-Musk tried to convince the courtroom he was misunderstood. "That did not go over well," Krysta Yang said on the Kit and Krysta podcast (via Techradar ). Yang was a former host of Nintendo Minute with Kit Ellis - the eponymous Kit in the podcast's title - and both worked within Nintendo for more than 10 years. "We were still there for that," Ellis added. "That was one that was not beloved by the people ... That was not received well at Nintendo," Yang echoed.. Ellis said the Wario sketch came out of "leftfield" because it wasn't obviously tethered to anything, as there wasn't a Mario or Wario game releasing at that time. "Why is Elon Musk Wario?" Ellis recalled people wondering. "Some of the stuff was getting into subject matter that was uncomfortable for Nintendo." Nintendo had nothing to do with the sketch, the pair insisted, "But there is a lot of contact between Nintendo and the producers of SNL, [and] these other late night shows. There are people who are very focused on that segment in particular within the communications team at Nintendo, making sure that they get games when they come out, that they have access to information." In the most recent Zelda vs. GTA 6 sketch, Link and Jason - main characters in their respective games - argue about whose game is best. Yang and Ellis praised Link's costume - "This seemed to be custom-made to the remake," Ellis said - but the pair were more muted on the skit itself. "I thought this was generally fine," Yang said. "I wasn't rolling on the floor laughing or anything like that. There were some moments where it's a little cringey." The Ocarina of Time remake was shown in some detail in September, ahead of its 5th November release. The game's art style has been updated considerably, which has been a topic of much debate , but there are changes to performance and to the ways the game works, as well. It's a notable undertaking. Meanwhile, GTA 6 looms large for its 19th November release.

stories.title: A New '3 for 2' Board Game Sale Is Now Live at Amazon and Target

sources.name: IGN
sources.title: A New '3 for 2' Board Game Sale Is Now Live at Amazon and Target
sources.text: If you’ve been eager to build up your tabletop collection for some fall game nights, you’re in luck: Target and Amazon are both running hefty ‘3 for 2’ sales on board games, puzzles, and toys. I took some time to compare selections between the two sales, and Target actually comes out on top in terms of just how many options are includedin the deal. However, if you’re looking for a specific game, you may find a better individual discount at Amazon. The massive retailer just had its October Prime Day sale last week, and some discounts haven’t gone away just yet. Both sales work in the same way: Add three eligible items to your cart, and the cheapest of the three will be automatically discounted to $0 at checkout. I’d recommend some strategy around the price of the three items you include to maximize that “cheapest item” discount. The deal also stacks, so you’ll get one free game or puzzle for every three you add to your cart. Both sales include a mix of both traditional tabletop and more quick-playing card games. If you don’t already have something in mind, I’d think about whether your collection is missing something quick and casual or a longer campaign for a more dedicated group. If you’re just trying to build up a solid collection, you’ll never regret picking up classics like Catan . There’s also a splattering of themed editions. These include, of course, ridiculous amounts of Monopoly variants, though you also have entirely new franchise releases like the Fourth Wing board game . As someone who gets way too much satisfaction out of knowing the Pokedex, I’d personally recommend the Pokemon edition of Guess Who . Why do I think Target takes the win on this one? Well, besides including classics like Clue that Amazon skipped out on, Target is also including tons of expansions. So instead of getting three separate games, you could get Cards Against Humanity plus two of its expansions. Or you could just invest in a bunch of expansions for games you already own. Both sales also include tons of jigsaw puzzles from major companies like Ravensburger, RoseArt, and theory11. Sure, these might not offer the same level of competition as a board game, but they still offer an opportunity for some social collaboration. Blythe (she/her) is an Audience Development Coordinator at IGN who spends way too much time in character customization screens and tracking down collectibles.

sources.name: IGN
sources.title: Satisfactory: The Board Game Preview
sources.text: Automation and factory-building games have become pretty popular over the past few years, with Coffee Stain Studios' Satisfactory being one of the stars of the genre. I have always admired the sprawling conveyor belts and mega structures of the factory-building powerhouse from a comfortable distance, dipping my toe into the waters with messy (but kind of functional) factories of my own. Soon, factory builders will have a whole new way to build out their process, as Mood Publishing, the same publisher behind Hitman: The Board Game , is looking to bring the beloved factory sim to your tabletop with Satisfactory: The Board Game and the launch of their latest crowdfunding campaign over on Gamefound . We were sent an early prototype copy to check out, in addition to playing a demo with the game’s designer, David Thor Fjalarsson, to see if a tabletop game can capture and refine the Satisfactory experience down to the size of a kitchen table-sized factory. In Satisfactory: The Board Game (referred to simply as "Satisfactory" going forward), designed by David Thor Fjalarsson, up to four players will have to mine, refine, and upgrade their factories in an effort to earn the most FICSIT points before the space elevator is finished. The turns themselves are surprisingly straightforward; on your turn, you will perform two actions, either build something, move around the map, or have your factory do its work. Once each player has taken their turn, the production phase occurs, where everyone's mines will activate, drilling for one of the three basic materials—limestone, iron, or copper—and existing materials will move down their conveyors towards getting refined into better resources. Then, the whole cycle repeats itself. Even in my first game, by the time my group had reached the second or third round, we had the flow down. The game itself takes place on a large hex-grid representation of the video game's massive world, with random creatures and biomes that get placed during setup, along with various material-rich points where mines can be placed. The “Move” action is pretty self-explanatory, allowing you to move your piece up to a number of spaces equal to your movement value, with some spaces that can only be crossed once certain technologies or vehicles have been built. Landing on a point can grant you resources, or allow you to claim one of the tokens mentioned earlier. If you prefer to get some extra work in at your factories, you can instead opt for the “Workshop” action, which lets you either move a beltline of resources down a spot or refine a single block of material into a higher-tier version, which is a crucial component for when you build. Speaking of building things, the “Build” action was my favorite, and what I would consider the core thing to do in this game. At any time, players will have access to build their staple devices—extractors, refineries, et cetera—in addition to a random pool of cards of varying tiers that get unlocked over the course of the game. These cards, like the Jet Pack to help you get around quicker or weapons to tackle the wildlife, are a great help, but the main structures you can construct have an added little treat to them. Depending on what you build, you will have a bonus action that you can take, determined by what you have built. Building a miner, for instance, will allow you to immediately build a Belt, which will then trigger the Belt’s bonus, giving you a free movement action, or the Constructor, giving you an extra action you can take on your turn. Stringing together these bonuses to create some wild turns was some of the most fun I had playing Satisfactory. When it comes to playing, Satisfactory's tabletop adaptation has opted for a competitive “race for points” experience for its main game, instead of the cooperative focus from the PC title — though the promised final game will include a co-op and solo modes as well. That said, don't expect to be bombing or taking out the other players' extractors and belts with some cardboard corporate terrorism within the game. Instead, once a player has claimed a tile by building something on it, no other player can develop on it, though they can still cross over with no issue. Satisfactory can still be “mean,” but it’s more like cleverly getting in the way or making expansion for your opponents annoying as opposed to turning the planet into a battlefield. This sort of headbutting really only comes out when you start getting to the three- or four-player counts. At two players, because both players have so much more space, I was surprised and impressed with how different Satisfactory manages to feel. During my two-player game, with far less worry about my factory getting locked in by other players, I instead was able to focus and work out how best I wanted to try and optimize (as optimized as you could get in a game like this after only a couple plays) my system. It honestly felt like I was playing different games based on the player counts, with two players focusing on optimizing and planning out turns to maximize earning points, while with three, and especially four, figuring out how best to expand my factory and balancing blocking resources from the others was much more in the forefront of my mind. Oddly enough, I think I actually enjoyed the puzzley nature of the lower player count more, as both of us weren’t forced into conflict with one another, and I could better test out what Satisfactory offers. In one two-player game, I focused on maxing out my basic resource production, getting all of my extractors online as fast as I could, and expanding my reach to a few farther-out “rich” tiles, which further let me produce more of the resource during production phases. Having an almost overabundance of these cheaper resources allowed me to quickly gobble up and complete the early-game Milestones, netting me a bunch of points and rocketing me out into the lead, faster than the elevator could take me. sources.title: Star Wars Galactic Racer's devs tested its roguelite progression system by turning it into a board game
sources.text: "You can't know if you can feel the system until you can play the system." Years ago, I read that Jake Solomon prototyped the Firaxis reboot of XCOM by making a simple board game version. Something rudimentary that could be played in the office on scrap paper to get ideas across and figure out where the fun would be, without having to commit. But it's surprising to hear the same idea being used for a game as different from XCOM's turn-based tactics as Star Wars Galactic Racer. As Fuse Games' creative director Kieran Crimmins told Eurogamer , "You can't know if you can feel the system until you can play the system." And so the early prototype of this high-speed arcade racing game was indeed a board game. "You know, modern engines are so capable that you can do a lot of it in-software," CEO Matt Webster said, "but there's still something [about that which is] not as fast as getting a written idea down. From a board game perspective, you sort of decouple yourself from a particular prototype and you're talking about moment-to-moment." Specifically, the board game simulated Galactic Racer's progression system. Its rewards differ based on the event, but typically offer tuning points to spend on one of three random stats, and maybe a part for your speeder that will affect its abilities or grant a bonus related to a specific status effect. After several races you get to go shopping, and spend the credits you've earned on more upgrades and parts, or a whole new ability. It's a progression system right out of a roguelite, with new unlocks added to a pool so they might appear in future runs, and each run handing out tuning points that can be used for permanent upgrades that carry over between them. Not something you expect in a racing game, and a system that presumably needed a bit of road testing to find the fun. "There's a prototyping tool for every kind of system that you want to prototype," Crimmins said, "and the one that you pick should be the one that gets you there the quickest, and gets you to validate the emotion the quickest. So when it came to upgrades and meta progression, I can do a board game in a day. I mean, I say 'board game'. A lot of it is Post-its and a scribble and some dice. But we're trying to validate those feelings as quickly as possible. So you just pick the best tool for the moment." 2026 games : All the upcoming games Best PC games : Our all-time favorites Free PC games : Freebie fest Best FPS games : Finest gunplay Best RPGs : Grand adventures Best co-op games : Better together Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team. Jody's first computer was a Commodore 64, so he remembers having to use a code wheel to play Pool of Radiance. A former music journalist who interviewed everyone from Giorgio Moroder to Trent Reznor, Jody also co-hosted Australia's first radio show about videogames, Zed Games . He's written for Rock Paper Shotgun , The Big Issue, GamesRadar , Zam , Glixel , Five Out of Ten Magazine , and Playboy.com , whose cheques with the bunny logo made for fun conversations at the bank. Jody's first article for PC Gamer was about the audio of Alien Isolation , published in 2015. Jody edited PC Gamer Indie from 2017 to 2018, and he eventually lived up to his promise to play every Warhammer videogame. sources.name: Gematsu
sources.title: Usual June delayed to January 20, 2027
sources.text: Finji has delayed supernatural third-person action adventure game Usual June from its previously planned October 28 release date to January 20, 2027. It will be available for PC via Steam . Here is an overview of the game, via Finji: Usual June is a third-person action adventure game where players can fight monsters, talk to ghosts, and most importantly get to the bottom of a mystery threatening to obliterate an entire city. Players will get to explore unique locations such as secret labs, buried tunnels, haunted observatories, abandoned train stations, and a beautiful but mysterious other world. Players will dive into arenas with fast, fluid, and expressive combat. While being able to dash, use super moves, dodge and parry, players will have to adapt to enemies and change June’s fighting style by equipping items and customizing loadout. As players get more XP and level up, they will gain access to new powers. But these powers come with a cost they will have to discover by themselves. As neither the living nor the dead can save this city on their own, players will get to talk to a colorful cast of 25 characters to get to the bottom of what is happening in Fen Harbor, using the photographic memories of the dead, and the living’s ability to touch things to find out what is happening before all the ghosts disappear and time runs out. Developed by the Finji team, Usual June is led by creative director Adam Saltsman ( Overland , Canabalt ), and produced in collaboration with writer David Pinckney ( Needle & Thread ), BAFTA winning writer Cara Ellison ( Ghost Town , The Seance of Blake Manor ) and BAFTA winning audio director Adam Hay ( Dreams , Everybody’s Gone to the Rapture ).
